item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau
item.content:encoded: Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18. Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday. “Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.” Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers). Even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data. Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances. “Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.” In addition to their suite of scientific instruments , the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record , a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it. “Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.” Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, transformed our understanding of the solar system through their exploration of the outer planets. In 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made spacecraft to enter interstellar space. On Nov. 18, 2026, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. Milestones, challenges Traveling about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), Voyager 1 in 2012 became the first spacecraft to leave the heliosphere , the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun that deflects cosmic radiation, and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2, taking a different trajectory, crossed the boundary in 2018. “The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.” Creative engineering solutions have enabled the probes to conserve energy and overcome challenges related to aging hardware, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer on the spacecraft. Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives — a move not without risk — to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator . Essentially a nuclear battery, the generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. With the plutonium supply continually depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer. As with all NASA spacecraft that venture to and beyond the Moon, communication between Earth and the Voyager probes is managed by the agency’s Deep Space Network , large antennas located at three facilities around the world. “We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.” For more information about NASA’s Voyager mission, visit: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/ -end- Abbey Interrante / Karen Fox Headquarters, Washington 202-358-1600 abbey.a.interrante@nasa.gov / karen.c.fox@nasa.gov Calla Cofield Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif. 626-808-2469 calla.e.cofield@jpl.nasa.gov Share Details Last Updated Nov 19, 2026 Editor Jessica Taveau Location NASA Headquarters Related Terms Voyager 1 Heliophysics Heliophysics Division Jet Propulsion Laboratory Science Mission Directorate The Solar System The Sun

item.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things
item.description: Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 There's something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it's the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watched other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn't watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature. The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them. The ninth day was "fight night," when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents' excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously. Read full article Comments

item.title: Qualcomm offers test drive of its rack-scale Nvidia AI challenger
item.description: Qualcomm has opened cloud-based trials of its Dragonfly AI200 rack-scale inference system to selected customers through Cirrascale Cloud Services. Dragonfly AI200 is Qualcomm's pitch for running large language, multimodal, and other AI models without Nvidia-sized power and operating bills. Whether it delivers those savings is something customers can now put to the test on Cirrascale's AI Innovation Cloud, with a route into production deployments, Qualcomm says. Cirrascale also demonstrated the system at SC26 in Chicago on November 17-18. The AI200 is part of Qualcomm's Dragonfly datacenter lineup, which also includes the AI250 and AI300 accelerators and the C1000 server CPU. The company set out its broader ambitions at its Investor Day in June . Each AI200 accelerator card carries 768 GB of LPDDR memory, with 56 cards providing about 43 TB in a liquid-cooled rack. Qualcomm says the system supports models ranging from 7 billion to 10 trillion parameters, including long-context, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic workloads. As we previously explored , packing in memory doesn't necessarily mean matching Nvidia's performance. Its Blackwell-based NVL72 systems use fast – and costly – HBM3e stacks, while Qualcomm has opted for LPDDR, more commonly found in mobile devices. "AI inference is becoming one of the largest and most important computing workloads in the datacenter, and the industry needs a more efficient approach," said Tony Pialis, Qualcomm's executive vice president and general manager for datacenter. He claimed that the AI200 brings the company's experience with high-performance, low-power computing to a rack-scale infrastructure, in an architecture designed around the performance, memory, and cost requirements of inference workloads. "Our customers need efficient, scalable infrastructure that can support increasingly sophisticated models without allowing power and operating costs to become the limiting factor," said Cirrascale CEO Dave Driggers. "By working with Qualcomm, we can give customers evaluation access to a compelling new architecture purpose-built for the next generation of AI inference." The chip firm also has its own software stack, the Dragonfly AI Infrastructure Management Suite, for provisioning, monitoring, workload orchestration, and fault handling across rack-scale deployments. ®

item.title: Leonid meteor shower thrills stargazers worldwide with colorful sky show (photos/video)
item.description: null The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it. The annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot. And for some, their patience certainly paid off. Leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light. The meteor shower is also famous for producing some of the most spectacular meteor storms in history. In fact, this year marks the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, when observers reported an astonishing 40 meteors per second at the peak. To mark the occasion, we spoke to people who witnessed the extraordinary event first-hand and you can read their remarkable accounts in our special feature . But back to the present! Let's take a look at some of the best photographs and videos captured during this year's impressive display. Photographer Austin Rebello drove several hours to Nubble Lighthouse in York, Maine, to meet up with fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright and hopefully capture a Leonid or two. "I specifically drove a few hours up there for hopes of capturing exactly this, as the radiant of the Leonids rose behind the lighthouse," Rebello told Space.com in an email. Leonid meteor streaks over Nubble Lighthouse, York, Maine. (Image credit: Austin Rebello) "My friend and I were lucky enough to also see it with our eyes, and it was definitely a top 3 meteor for me, as it was even bright enough to briefly cast shadows." A close up view of a Leonid meteor. (Image credit: Austin Rebello) Rebello also revealed on X that the meteor left behind a vibrant blue trail that remained visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds. The meteor left a vibrant blue streak that was visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds. (Image credit: Austin Rebello) Fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright was also at Nubble Lighthouse that night, where he captured the lingering trail of a particularly bright meteor on camera for an incredible 12 minutes, according to a post on X. "Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there," Wright wrote on X . Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there. I was able to make a rough timelapse video to show this.--November 18, 2026York, Maine https://t.co/pm9htHcMm3 November 18, 2026 This phenomenon is known as a persistent meteor train and is created when a bright meteor leaves behind a trail of ionized gas that continues to glow long after the meteor itself has disappeared. A close up view of a Leonid meteor. The meteor left a vibrant blue streak that was visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds. Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there. I was able to make a rough timelapse video to show this.--November 18, 2026York, Maine https://t.co/pm9htHcMm3 November 18, 2026 This phenomenon is known as a persistent meteor train and is created when a bright meteor leaves behind a trail of ionized gas that continues to glow long after the meteor itself has disappeared. These ghostly trails usually fade relatively quickly, but some, like this one, can persist for several minutes. They can twist and change shape as they're carried along by winds high in Earth's atmosphere, according to the BBC Sky at Night Magazine . Meanwhile, over Deming, New Mexico, photographer Greg Gage had to contend with rather less favorable conditions as clouds and unexpected fog rolled in during the meteor shower's peak. A bright Leonid meteor streaks through the star-studded sky above Deming, New Mexico. (Image credit: Greg Gage) "While it was perfectly clear when I set up the camera, the night turned out to be mostly cloudy with some light fog," Gage told Space.com in an email. "But it was just a thin veil and made for some interesting effects. I did catch one meteor through the fog." A bright Leonid meteor made itself visible despite the tricky fog and cloud conditions. (Image credit: Greg Gage) But the fog wasn't the only surprise Gage encountered. He also managed to capture a particularly colorful meteor as it blazed through the sky. "One meteor was rather dramatic. It went through multiple colors as it traveled through the atmosphere," Gage continued. Gage captured the photographs with a Nikon D5500 and a 14mm lens. A close up view of a colorful Leonid meteor streaking through the sky above Deming, New Mexico. (Image credit: Greg Gage) And the colorful displays weren't limited to North America. In Japan, astronomer Daichi Fujii, curator of the Hiratsuka City Museum, captured a spectacular Leonid fireball streaking across the sky above Hiratsuka in the early hours of Nov. 19. The brilliant fireball left behind a glowing trail that changed from green to orange as it lingered in the sky. さきほど、しし座流星群の大火球が流れました。2026年11月19日4時35分2秒に、平塚から北の低い空に向けたカメラでとらえた様子です。緑色のアフターグローからオレンジ色の永続痕まで、美しく色を変化させました。 https://t.co/Q5ihqCPtX2 November 18, 2026 A fireball is defined as an unusually bright meteor that reaches a visual magnitude of -3 or brighter, according to NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies. Elsewhere in Japan, skywatcher @simao had a particularly productive night, capturing an impressive 92 meteors between 10:17 p.m. local time on Nov. 18 and 5:40 a.m. on Nov. 19, from central Saitama Prefecture. 昨夜から今朝にかけて捉えた流星は正味92個でした。11/18 22:17 〜 11/19 05:40埼玉県中央から #atomcam #meteordetect #火球 #流星 https://t.co/jRzsHdQ7MV November 19, 2026 But that wasn't all simao captured that night! At 2:19 a.m. on Nov. 19, they caught both a Leonid meteor and a sprite at the same time, looking northwest. Sprites are very difficult to capture, as they appear as fleeting flashes of light high above thunderstorms, typically appearing as red, jellyfish-like structures. 昨夜の流星とスプライト、初めて同じタイミングで撮れた。11/19 02:19:36埼玉県中央から北西の空 #atomcam #meteordetect #火球 #流星 #スプライト https://t.co/LBipTuoM0L November 19, 2026 The Leonids were already making an appearance in the days leading up to the shower's peak. On Nov. 16, astrophotographer @EricTheSpaceCat captured several possible Leonids streaking through the sky. Meteors from last night/this morning.Cropped to show detail.A lot of possible Leonids. The Leonid meteor shower is active and peaks the night of 11/17-11/18. https://t.co/s7YsvKdvEC November 15, 2026 A likely Leonid meteor from yesterday morning.The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight! Good luck if you go out to watch. https://t.co/xxbEV32NQl November 17, 2026 If the Leonids have left you wanting more, you won't have to wait long for another significant meteor shower! Next up are the Geminids , one of the most prolific meteor showers of the year, which will peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. And 2026 is shaping up to be a particularly good year for them. With only a slender waxing crescent moon in the sky, moonlight interference will be minimal, giving skywatchers a chance to spot up to 120 Geminid meteors per hour under ideal conditions. For the best views, head somewhere dark, away from city lights, and give your eyes around 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness. Editor's Note: If you snap an impressive night sky photo and would like to share it with Space.com's readers, send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: Nonprofit Common Space will launch 1st 'humanitarian satellite' in 2027
item.description: null The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to plan. The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites , whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world. That plan firmed up a bit today (Nov. 19), as Common Space announced the builder of the first of those satellites : Satellogic, an Argentine-U.S. geospatial intelligence company. There are more than 1,000 Earth-observing satellites circling our planet at the moment. But much of the data they gather is proprietary or too expensive to serve the common good, according to Common Space. The nonprofit wants to change that via its envisioned constellation, which it says will collect imagery specifically for humanitarian and public-interest purposes. Common Space plans to operate on a "club-good model," which will share infrastructure and costs across a large community, allowing extensive, low-cost access to high-quality imagery. Satellogic is now officially part of this picture. "With Satellogic as our spacecraft partner, we're moving from vision to orbit and putting high-resolution data into the hands of those who need it most," Common Space co-founder Rhiannan Price said in a statement today. "This isn't just another satellite. We're building infrastructure to serve people for years to come." The satellite is Satellogic's NewSat Mark V, which Common Space selected after a competitive request-for-proposal process. Satellites can help first responders deal with natural disasters. Here, one of Vantor's Earth-imaging satellites captures the destruction Hurricane Melissa caused to Black River, in southwest Jamaica, in November 2025. (Image credit: Vantor Technologies/CC BY 4.0) The NewSat Mark V is just 32 inches (82 centimeters) long and weighs 85 pounds (38.5 kilograms) here on Earth . But the microsatellite packs a great deal of capability into that small package. From low Earth orbit (LEO), it naturally resolves features on the ground as small as 27.5 inches (70 cm), which Satellogic's proprietary algorithms can boost to a "super resolution" of 19.7 inches (50 cm). The satellite is scheduled to launch in July 2027, on a rocket that has yet to be announced. Satellogic will handle the preparations for that launch and manage satellite operations, which are expected to last at least five years in LEO. The company has extensive experience with such work; it has flown 61 of its Earth-observing satellites to date, all of which deployed successfully. And Satellogic is aligned with Common Space philosophically, the company stressed. "Common Space shares our belief that persistent global intelligence shouldn't be reserved for a few. Humanitarian responders and journalists are often first on the ground and last to get access, yet they need frequent, high-resolution imagery to see what's really happenin

item.content:encoded: null The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to plan. The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites , whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world. That plan firmed up a bit today (Nov. 19), as Common Space announced the builder of the first of those satellites : Satellogic, an Argentine-U.S. geospatial intelligence company. There are more than 1,000 Earth-observing satellites circling our planet at the moment. But much of the data they gather is proprietary or too expensive to serve the common good, according to Common Space. The nonprofit wants to change that via its envisioned constellation, which it says will collect imagery specifically for humanitarian and public-interest purposes. Common Space plans to operate on a "club-good model," which will share infrastructure and costs across a large community, allowing extensive, low-cost access to high-quality imagery. Satellogic is now officially part of this picture. "With Satellogic as our spacecraft partner, we're moving from vision to orbit and putting high-resolution data into the hands of those who need it most," Common Space co-founder Rhiannan Price said in a statement today. "This isn't just another satellite. We're building infrastructure to serve people for years to come." The satellite is Satellogic's NewSat Mark V, which Common Space selected after a competitive request-for-proposal process. Satellites can help first responders deal with natural disasters. Here, one of Vantor's Earth-imaging satellites captures the destruction Hurricane Melissa caused to Black River, in southwest Jamaica, in November 2025. (Image credit: Vantor Technologies/CC BY 4.0) The NewSat Mark V is just 32 inches (82 centimeters) long and weighs 85 pounds (38.5 kilograms) here on Earth . But the microsatellite packs a great deal of capability into that small package. From low Earth orbit (LEO), it naturally resolves features on the ground as small as 27.5 inches (70 cm), which Satellogic's proprietary algorithms can boost to a "super resolution" of 19.7 inches (50 cm). The satellite is scheduled to launch in July 2027, on a rocket that has yet to be announced. Satellogic will handle the preparations for that launch and manage satellite operations, which are expected to last at least five years in LEO. The company has extensive experience with such work; it has flown 61 of its Earth-observing satellites to date, all of which deployed successfully. And Satellogic is aligned with Common Space philosophically, the company stressed. "Common Space shares our belief that persistent global intelligence shouldn't be reserved for a few. Humanitarian responders and journalists are often first on the ground and last to get access, yet they need frequent, high-resolution imagery to see what's really happening so they can act with confidence," Luciano Giesso, vice president of space systems at Satellogic, said in the same statement. "This mission puts our vision of democratized access into practice." Common Space is currently raising money to expand the constellation to six satellites, which it hopes to have in place by 2030. This will allow daily high-resolution coverage of "priority areas," according to the nonprofit. Editor's note: The original version of this story stated that the first Satellogic satellite will launch on a SpaceX rocket. This information was in an embargoed version of today's press release but was not in the final version, so it has been removed from this story.

item.title: Voyager 1 celebrates one light-day with a nice lie-down
item.description: Voyager 1 marked its milestone of one light-day from Earth in time-honored fashion: by giving controllers the silent treatment. On November 14, the mission team noticed that the veteran spacecraft had stopped returning science and engineering data. A Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra, Australia, picked up its carrier signal, but no data. The carrier signal indicates that Voyager 1 can still keep its antenna pointed at Earth and operate its transmitting equipment. However, something could be amiss with the system responsible for collecting and collating data from the spacecraft. Something similar happened in 2023 . After a few months of troubleshooting, engineers managed to coax a response from the probe, and by June 2024, NASA was delighted to announce that the spacecraft was back in action. The problem was traced to a faulty computer chip, and engineers devised a software update to work around the defective hardware. That experience will stand the team in good stead this time around. There was also a brief interruption in communications with Voyager 1 in October, which could have been caused by the spacecraft dropping into safe mode after a thruster failover occurred. Engineers are investigating whether the two incidents are connected. The Voyagers have an impressive amount of fault protection built in, which has contributed to their extraordinary longevity. It will be half a century in 2027 since the spacecraft were launched, so glitches are understandable and likely. NASA expects to confirm on November 19 that Voyager 1 was still operating when it reached one light-day from Earth on November 18, using its carrier signal and trajectory calculations. The day's delay neatly illustrates a major headache for engineers: communication latency. It now takes more than 24 hours for commands to reach the spacecraft, and the same amount of time for a response to be received. Diagnosing the fault could therefore take weeks or longer. ®

item.title: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child
item.description: Rockstar Games’ brilliant 18-rated criminal caper is stuffed with sex, drugs and violence. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “ no way” . Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty. Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple , Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Continue reading...

item.title: From Tunde Kelani to Akinola Davies Jr., 5 Nollywood Directors You Should Know
item.description: From music visuals to international festival stages and actor-turned-director debuts, Dammy Twitch, Akinola Davies Jr., and Daniel Etim Effiong represent different paths into Nollywood directing. Think about the Nigerian films and series you have watched recently, the ones that kept you glued to your screen, had you talking about the storyline long after the credits rolled or recommending them to everyone you know. While the actors are often the faces you remember first, there is someone behind the camera whose creative choices help bring those stories to life: the director. From interpreting the script and guiding actors to shaping how each scene looks, sounds and unfolds, directors influence almost every part of what ends up on screen. As Nollywood grows in ambition, production quality and global reach, the filmmakers steering these projects are becoming just as central to the industry’s story as the stars in front of the lens. Some have spent decades bringing Nigerian literature and history to the screen, while others are earning international acclaim or crossing over from music videos into feature films. Here are five Nollywood directors whose work is worth knowing. Tunde Kelani Start with Tunde Kelani if you want to see where modern Nigerian cinema found its literary and cultural roots. Trained at the London Film School after cutting his teeth in photography and television, the Mainframe Films founder has spent decades turning Nigerian literature, stage plays, and history into lasting screen works. Titles like Ti Oluwa Nile , Koseegbe , O Le Ku , Saworoide , Thunderbolt: Magun , The Narrow Path , Maami , Dazzling Mirage , Ayinla , and Cordelia show how wide his range goes. Across years of festivals and awards, Kelani has collected major honours for his craft, and his adaptation Cordelia earned him a Best Director nomination at the 2026 Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards. Tunde Kelani, whose directing catalogue spans Ti Oluwa Nile, Saworoide, The Narrow Path, Maami, and Cordelia, with Kunle Afolayan outdoors. Photo Credit: Tunde Kelani/Instagram Akinola Davies Jr. Few directors have linked global festival stages with homegrown Nollywood triumphs quite like Akinola Davies Jr. After his short film Lizard won the Short Film Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival in 2021, he co-wrote and directed his feature debut My Father’s Shadow alongside his brother Wale Davies . The drama made history in 2025 as the first Nigerian film selected for the Official Selection at the Cannes Film Festival, picking up a Special Mention for the Caméra d’Or before winning Best Director at the British Independent Film Awards and Breakthrough Director at the Gotham Independent Film Awards. His momentum rolled straight into 2026 with a BAFTA win for Outstanding Debut by a British Writer, Director or Producer, followed by Best Director and Best Overall Movie wins at the 2026 AMVCAs. Akinola Davies Jr. with his BAFTA trophy for My Father’s Shadow. Photo Credit: A

Tunde Kelani, whose directing catalogue spans Ti Oluwa Nile, Saworoide, The Narrow Path, Maami, and Cordelia, with Kunle Afolayan outdoors. Photo Credit: Tunde Kelani/Instagram Akinola Davies Jr. Few directors have linked global festival stages with homegrown Nollywood triumphs quite like Akinola Davies Jr. After his short film Lizard won the Short Film Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival in 2021, he co-wrote and directed his feature debut My Father’s Shadow alongside his brother Wale Davies . The drama made history in 2025 as the first Nigerian film selected for the Official Selection at the Cannes Film Festival, picking up a Special Mention for the Caméra d’Or before winning Best Director at the British Independent Film Awards and Breakthrough Director at the Gotham Independent Film Awards. His momentum rolled straight into 2026 with a BAFTA win for Outstanding Debut by a British Writer, Director or Producer, followed by Best Director and Best Overall Movie wins at the 2026 AMVCAs. Akinola Davies Jr. with his BAFTA trophy for My Father’s Shadow. Photo Credit: Akinola Davies Jr./Instagram Kemi Adetiba Before crossing into cinema and streaming, Kemi Adetiba built a reputation directing memorable music videos for artists including Wizkid , Tiwa Savage , Olamide , and Banky W . On the big screen, she shattered box-office records with The Wedding Party and followed up with the crime drama King of Boys , its sequel King of Boys: The Return of the King , and the series To Kill a Monkey . Her sharp pacing, bold casting, and distinct visual style have kept her in the spotlight across platforms such as The Headies, the City People Entertainment Awards, and the AMVCAs. Kemi Adetiba and Bucci Franklin on the set of To Kill a Monkey. Photo Credit: Kemi Adetiba/Instagram Daniel Etim Effiong Many movie lovers know Daniel Etim Effiong first as a familiar leading man across Nollywood films and streaming hits, yet his work behind the camera is just as central to his career. Having studied filmmaking at AFDA in South Africa and gained experience on shorts and television episodes, he stepped into feature directing with the thriller The Herd . That debut brought him Best Director and Best Debut Feature Film by a Director nominations at the 2026 Africa Movie Academy Awards, while The Herd collected three AMAA trophies and earned nine AMVCA nominations, including Best Director. Daniel Etim Effiong on the set of The Herd which leads the 12th AMVCA nominations with 9 nods including Best Director. Dammy Twitch Known for years for directing visually bold music videos for stars like Davido , Burna Boy , and Omah Lay , Dammy Twitch ( Apampa Oluwadamilola Owolabi ) made his feature film directing debut in May 2026 with the romantic comedy Call of My Life . Led by Uzoamaka Power and Andrew Yaw Bunting alongside Zubby Michael , Beverly Osu , Nkem Owoh , Patience Ozokwor , and Broda Shaggi , the film crossed ₦900 million at the Nigerian box office to become one of the highest-grossing Nollywood releases of 2026, while also winning the Favourite Feature Narrative Audience Award at the 2026 BlackStar Film Festival. Bringing his instincts for framing, colour, and pacing from music visuals into narrative cinema, he has quickly become a fresh voice movie fans are keeping a close eye on. Dammy Twitch on the set of Call of My Life. item.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
item.description: The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it. But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. It’s just a noise, but it’s unmistakably Danny Kelly. He regains the power of speech and follows it up with: “Gooooaaaal … Goalll Stan, Goalll at the Emirates.” Reporter Ian Abrahams and Stan Collymore join the excitement, before Danny comes back: “I LOVE FOOTBALL, STAN, I LOVE IT.” It is such a brilliant piece of radio . From one of the absolute greats. Continue reading...

item.title: Microsoft To Do will soon become Microsoft Done
item.description: Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago. The confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and plans for Copilot and Microsoft 365. Until now, there was To Do or Planner (in basic or premium guise). The idea is "a single system for tracking your work as an individual, as a team, and as an organization." To Do contributes features to that future, but its apps don't get to join it. The problem is that Planner doesn't do everything To Do does. Microsoft would like users to migrate to Planner but, by the company's own admission , there are plenty of gaps. No native Windows or Mac desktop apps are planned to replace To Do; file attachments aren't supported on tasks in the Planner private plan, and there's no equivalent to To Do list groups in Planner. "Equivalent To Do printing and email-list capabilities are not currently planned for the replacement experience," and so on. Existing To Do tasks and lists won't migrate to Planner either. They'll remain accessible through Planner until June 30, 2027, but that access ends with the apps. Microsoft says the date does not itself trigger deletion of the underlying data. Personal Microsoft account holders are left in an even worse state: Planner isn't available to them, including Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscribers. Microsoft's advice is to choose another task-management app and prepare to export their data. Export instructions are still to come, and exporting won't necessarily produce something another app can import. Very much a case of "don't let the door hit you on the way out." Unifying tasks and plans is a good idea – the current situation does create confusion, as Microsoft acknowledged. However, taking an axe to To Do, which was developed to be a successor to Wunderlist ( acquired in 2015 for a figure between $100 million and $200 million, an early action under Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella), seems extreme. Microsoft calls the replacement "a unified platform for people and agents across Microsoft 365" and stated: "This unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier." Some users responding to the announcement were unimpressed, with one declaring "What a mess," and another asking if To Do might be spun off into an open source project: "Not everything needs to be put into an AI/Copilot agent." Indeed, it doesn't. But a useful service that doesn't ram Copilot and AI integration down customers' throats at every opportunity? That would never do. The message for To Do users appears to be: Get with the Plan(ner) or just get out. ®

item.title: Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’
item.description: Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under‑21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one. Time to talk, so let’s start with Tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and reckons he might have liked law, yet even that wasn’t his chosen field. Continue reading...

item.title: Cyberattack on service provider exposes payee data at 40 Irish credit unions
item.description: An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them. Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days. Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable." News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday. Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6. Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days. The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them. The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types: Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames Business Identifier Codes (BICs) International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) Sort codes Payment references Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers Payee addresses Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds. St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach. The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data." He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities. Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations. "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses." Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services. Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said. Credit unions operate similar

Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable." News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday. Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6. Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days. The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them. The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types: Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames Business Identifier Codes (BICs) International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) Sort codes Payment references Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers Payee addresses Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds. St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach. The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data." He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities. Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations. "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses." Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services. Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said. Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations. Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time. "What's most important is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he said. Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday. The FCA said October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing new rules. ®

item.title: What's next for NASA interstellar Voyager 1 probe after passing 1 light-day from Earth?
item.description: null Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft. Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2 , launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s. Voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035. So what's next for the two Voyager spacecraft as they reach further into interstellar space? Exploring afar Interstellar space, which is the area where the sun's constant stream of solar particles within the heliopause gives way to the physics of interstellar space, has been a valuable harvest for both Voyagers. Voyager 1 crossed interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to get data, while Voyager 2 has done the same since November 2018. "Current science is continuing our investigation on magnetic field strength and direction, plasma density, and energetic particle detection. What is important is to measure how these phenomena change as the spacecraft travels further away from the sun," Suzanne Dodd, project manager for the Voyager missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Space.com in an email. Added to that will be the Voyagers' examinations of plasma and magnetic fields nearby the spacecraft, and a focus on any "solar effects" such as shocks or pressure fronts, added JPL project scientist Linda Spilker in an email. "Key Voyager science going forward includes observing the extent to which our sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1," Spilker continued. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question." The team also wants to watch the magnetic field around the spacecraft continue to change direction from the sun, to interstellar space, Spilker noted. That finding was not expected when the Voyagers launched, so scientists are curious to know more — as long as the spacecraft can last, that is. Levay (STScI)) Power management Each Voyager continues to lose 4 watts of power a year; their launch power was 470 watts in 1977, and the nuclear power source continues to dwindle, requiring harder choices as the missions approach their 50th years of operations. item.content:encoded: null Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft. Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2 , launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s. Voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035. So what's next for the two Voyager spacecraft as they reach further into interstellar space? Exploring afar Interstellar space, which is the area where the sun's constant stream of solar particles within the heliopause gives way to the physics of interstellar space, has been a valuable harvest for both Voyagers. Voyager 1 crossed interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to get data, while Voyager 2 has done the same since November 2018. "Current science is continuing our investigation on magnetic field strength and direction, plasma density, and energetic particle detection. What is important is to measure how these phenomena change as the spacecraft travels further away from the sun," Suzanne Dodd, project manager for the Voyager missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Space.com in an email. Added to that will be the Voyagers' examinations of plasma and magnetic fields nearby the spacecraft, and a focus on any "solar effects" such as shocks or pressure fronts, added JPL project scientist Linda Spilker in an email. "Key Voyager science going forward includes observing the extent to which our sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1," Spilker continued. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question." The team also wants to watch the magnetic field around the spacecraft continue to change direction from the sun, to interstellar space, Spilker noted. That finding was not expected when the Voyagers launched, so scientists are curious to know more — as long as the spacecraft can last, that is. The locations of Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 beyond the boundary of our solar system. (Image credit: NASA, ESA, and Z. Levay (STScI)) Power management Each Voyager continues to lose 4 watts of power a year; their launch power was 470 watts in 1977, and the nuclear power source continues to dwindle, requiring harder choices as the missions approach their 50th years of operations. Instruments have had to be shut off, and both the spacecraft were directed to perform a "Big Bang" of power redistribution earlier this year to preserve as much power as possible without sacrificing science. Looking forward, Dodd says the team does not anticipate having to make any major changes to spacecraft operations until after the 50th anniversary passes for each spacecraft next August and September (as Voyager 2 launched a few weeks before Voyager 1). An image of Saturn captured by Voyager on Nov. 16, 1980 four days after the probe's closest approach to the planet, taken from a distance of 3,300,000 miles (5,300,000 kilometers). (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) A JPL representative added that the "Big Bang" should keep the remaining science instruments going until that point, although "there is also the thermal state of the spacecraft to balance." The representative added that the margins for power remain "very thin," especially as the spacecraft are quite cold in interstellar space. "Then there are the things the team can't predict, such as the unexpected loss of contact that happened recently," the spokesperson added, referring to an approximately 48-hour glitch in which Voyager 1 suddenly stopped responding to commands last month — although the spacecraft did quickly recover. "The goal of the mission is science, so the team is not just concerned with keeping in contact with the Voyagers, but keeping the science instruments going as long as possible," the representative added. "The further away the spacecraft get from Earth, the more they learn about how interstellar space changes further away from the heliopause." Voyager 2 in a clean room being worked on by engineers on March 23, 1977. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) The legacy of Voyager 1 Voyager 1 team members now represent multiple generations of engineers, each one of them with distinct but essential roles. Even the most junior members of the team—Nshan Kazaryan and Bhavana Gupta—are taking on key roles in anticipation of more responsibility in the future, according to JPL mission manager Kareem Badaruddin. "They have demonstrated their value to the team consistently," Badaruddin said in an email. Kazaryan's responsibilities include negotiating tracking schedules with the Deep Space Network (DSN), a set of three antennas for following distant missions, to keep tabs on the Voyagers. Gupta, meanwhile, has provided documentation to gather important details from the Voyagers' command and control systems to "give detailed instructions" in case of issues. "One of our most senior team members, Jack Lippincott, has provided critical knowledge and understanding of DSN operations and data interpretation," Badaruddin added. Pointing to one of the DSN antennas in Goldstone, California, he said the weather in that region "has been violent the last few weeks, and he has helped us to understand how to deal with unique problems that arose because of it." While there's no real sense of how much further the spacecraft could keep going, the team says it's committed to be there as long as possible. "It has taken decades of exceptional engineering to get Voyager 1 to the one light-day milestone, and hopefully much further before the mission ends," Dodd said. Badaruddin added: "One of the reasons that one light-day is so special is that it has never happened before that we were in contact with a spacecraft at this distance, and it may never happen again." Editor's note: This article was updated at 9 a.m. EST, Nov. 20, to correct the location of one of the DSN facilities to Goldstone, California (not Australia).

item.title: TfL takes Oyster photocard website offline after attackers compromise customer accounts
item.description: Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers. The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise. "We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," said Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident." TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did. TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected. Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over. Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too. TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems. Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action . There's no word yet on when it'll be back. "We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said. TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised. Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement

item.title: Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’
item.description: A 14-year civil war ravaged the country and ground women’s football to a halt. Today, the first glimmers of hope are beginning to emerge amid difficulty In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the title alive. Syria pulled out amid fears that the border would close. Back home, a war that had been largely frozen for four years was suddenly moving at pace. Rebel forces had swept out of the northwest, taking Aleppo and were pushing south towards the capital, 350km away, threatening to topple the now-former president, Bashar al-Assad. Players from the provinces around Damascus made their way home. But those from Hasakah, in the country’s far north-east, spent the next three days stranded at Damascus airport, as airline staff fled and planes sat idle on the tarmac, until a bus was finally able to take them home. Continue reading...

item.title: Esther Adeyanju: This International Men’s Day, Let’s Make Room for Men’s Vulnerability
item.description: “Men are not wired to show emotions.” A male friend once said to me during an argument. He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured. According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made. “So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed. He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature. Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine? The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.” Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard. Frequent questions men are asked: “How far? Work nko?” “When are you getting married?” “Have you bought land?” “How is the family?” And the famous Nigerian question that can make an unemployed graduate dread family gatherings: “So, what are you doing now?” We often inquire about their achievements, responsibilities, and plans. These aspects are important, but how often do we ask about their fears? A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about. We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean. Society has an interesting checklist for measuring a man’s success. A good job, a house, a car, a wife, children and financial stability. Preferably, all achieved before a certain age. But if a man struggles to achieve all these, is his life any less meaningful? Surely, a man’s worth cannot be reduced to his bank balance, job title or ability to convince everyone that he has everything under control. There must be room for men who are still becoming. A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about. We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean. Society has an interesting checklist for measuring a man’s success. A good job, a house, a car, a wife, children and financial stability. Preferably, all achieved before a certain age. But if a man struggles to achieve all these, is his life any less meaningful? Surely, a man’s worth cannot be reduced to his bank balance, job title or ability to convince everyone that he has everything under control. There must be room for men who are still becoming. The Empty Chair Nobody Notices This year’s theme for International Men’s Day, celebrated on November 19th, is “The Future Is Everyone.” While this theme may seem straightforward, it invites us to explore the true meaning of “everyone.” Working in corporate communications at the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management of Nigeria (CIPM) has heightened my awareness of how easily we categorise people based on their roles: leaders, employees, fathers, mothers, young professionals, and others. However, behind every label is a human being whose story is often more complex than it appears. The theme urges us to see people beyond face value, beyond titles and see them as humans first. It urges us to avoid assuming we know what others need. Allowing men to share their struggles does not diminish the experiences of another gender. Compassion is not a competition; there is ample space to challenge the expectations that confine both men and women. After all, what kind of future can belong to everyone if some individuals must conceal parts of themselves to fit in? This International Men’s Day, let’s celebrate the men who show up for their families, mentor young people, support their communities, and quietly make life better for others. Let’s remember the weary men—those who haven’t achieved everything they envisioned, who fear disappointing their families, and who desperately need help but have been taught that asking for assistance makes them less of a man. Reach out to your brother, check in on your father, and connect with that friend who always seems to have everything figured out. I still disagree with my friend’s belief that men were not created to show emotions. Men are human beings, not machines programmed to absorb every disappointment without showing vulnerability. If the future truly belongs to everyone, it must also include men who are allowed to be vulnerable, uncertain, imperfect, and human. We have spent generations teaching men to stand strong, but it’s time we remind them that they don’t always have to stand alone. item.title: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the company’s kingdom
item.description: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note. Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber , a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see. During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not. "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door." Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee. Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries. The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically. The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records. "At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said. After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in. The lessons here are pretty obvious. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note. Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber , a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see. During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not. "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door." Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee. Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries. The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically. The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records. "At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said. After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in. The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information. "The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®

item.title: Bank your stolen cash, bring a change of clothes, go easy on the bloodshed: 15 tips for playing Grand Theft Auto VI
item.description: There’s a vast amount to absorb in Leonida, but these pointers will rev up your criminal engines and allow you to better enjoy the ride Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? Leonida is so huge as to be overwhelming and in the opening hours, the game bombards you with tonnes of info that you will inevitably forget. But I’ve done nothing but play this game for weeks and I’m here to help. Here’s what I wished I’d known at the start Walk faster. I found that Jason and Lucia walk incredibly slowly. If you go into the options menu, you can select “fast walk” as the default walking speed, which sped them up just a little without ruining the pace or atmosphere of the game. While you’re in there, you can also customise plenty of other things, including controls and button mapping. Continue reading...

item.title: Burna Boy, Asake & Seyi Vibez Bring Afrobeats to the World of GTA VI
item.description: From left: Nigerian artists Asake, Seyi Vibez, and Burna Boy, whose songs appear in Grand Theft Auto VI. How else could Grand Theft Auto VI begin than with Nigerian artists featured in the music lineup of the biggest video game release of the year? As players around the world finally step into Rockstar Games’ highly anticipated open-world action-adventure title, Burna Boy , Asake , and Seyi Vibez are making sure Nigerian music is front and centre on the virtual streets of Vice City and the wider state of Leonida. Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) officially arrives today, Thursday, 19 November 2026, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, ending a 13-year wait since Grand Theft Auto V first hit consoles. Developed and published by Rockstar Games, the open-world action-adventure game follows dual protagonists Jason and Lucia across the sun-soaked, neon-lit state of Leonida—a fictional take on Florida that brings players back to Vice City in the franchise’s largest map yet. Music has always been at the heart of the Grand Theft Auto universe, where players tune into curated in-game radio stations while driving or walking around town, and this sixth instalment takes African soundscapes seriously. At the centre of the Nigerian presence is AfroBank FM, a dedicated African music radio station inside Grand Theft Auto VI that is co-hosted by Grammy winner Burna Boy—credited on-air simply as Burna—alongside British DJ and producer Palms Trax , who goes by Palmsy. Curated to spotlight everything from 20th-century African classics to contemporary Afrobeats, amapiano, and 3-step, the station features Asake’s 2022 hit “ Joha ” from his debut album Mr Money With The Vibe , as well as “ Giza “, the 2023 collaboration between Burna Boy and Seyi Vibez from Burna Boy’s seventh studio album I Told Them …. Alongside those tracks, Burna Boy also appears on the game’s official companion soundtrack album, Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, with his original song “ Bigger ” sitting on a 34-track roster that includes Travis Scott , Cardi B , Dua Lipa , SZA , Tame Impala , and Lana Del Rey . The African representation on AfroBank FM stretches beyond Nigeria too, sharing airwaves with Ghanaian highlife legends Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor on “ Gye Wani ” and South African stars DJ Lag , Robot Boii , and Kamo Mphela on “ Shay’sana “. With players able to listen to Leonida’s terrestrial radio stations both in vehicles and on foot through in-game headphones, millions of gamers worldwide are now cruising through Vice City with Burna Boy on the mic and Asake and Seyi Vibez on heavy rotation. The post Burna Boy, Asake & Seyi Vibez Bring Afrobeats to the World of GTA VI appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .
